What is MCP, and why not just use Notion's web connector? What lets a tool like Claude or ChatGPT read and write your own Notion is the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an open standard for connecting AI tools to external services.
The easiest path is the web version: both ChatGPT and Claude on the web can connect Notion with one OAuth click. But it has a privacy downside: that connection is tied to whatever account is logged in. If you share that AI account with family, anyone using the shared account can read your Notion through the AI.
Adding MCP to a tool on your own computer instead (Claude Code, Codex, and the like) avoids that: the authorization lives only in your machine's config, so someone logging into the shared web account can't reach it, and at authorization you can tick only the pages you want to expose, leaving the rest invisible.
Don't let "MCP" or "server" scare you: you host no server and install no extra packages. We use the MCP that Notion hosts officially, authorized over OAuth: add one config line, click approve in the browser, and the tool connects itself.
Connect Notion MCP in Claude Code: OAuth in three steps Notion's MCP offers two authentication methods, a pattern common to many MCP servers (GitHub's does the same): OAuth and a personal access token (PAT). This post leads with OAuth because it's the closest to Notion's recommended path: you connect to the server Notion hosts, with nothing to install or run locally and no extra package to maintain, and authorization is just a browser click. (For the PAT route, which gives tighter per-page control with the server on your own machine, there's a short section at the end.)
Step 1: Add it to Claude Code with one command Adding it is one line, over the HTTP transport pointed at Notion's official MCP URL:
1 claude mcp add --transport http notion https://mcp.notion.com/mcp It reports that it wrote to the local config:
1 2 Added HTTP MCP server notion with URL: https://mcp.notion.com/mcp to local config File modified: /home/wells/.claude.json [project: /home/wells] This line just records "which URL to connect to" into a local config file (~/.claude.json). It hasn't authorized anything yet. Without an explicit scope it applies to this project only, so add -s user to use it in every project.
(The URL comes in two flavors: mcp.notion.com/mcp is the newer streamable-HTTP endpoint most tools want, while mcp.notion.com/sse is for older clients that only speak SSE. --transport http with /mcp is the current standard.)
Step 2: Open Claude and run the browser authorization once Once the config is in, launch Claude Code by running claude in your terminal. On startup it prompts you to authenticate:
1 ⚠ 4 MCP servers need authentication · run /mcp Type /mcp in a session and you'll see notion flagged as needing authentication, so select it:
1 2 3 4 5 Manage MCP servers 9 servers Local MCPs (/home/wells/.claude.json [project: /home/wells]) ❯ notion · △ needs authentication Selecting it opens a browser for the OAuth flow (copy the URL manually if the browser doesn't open):
1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 Authenticating with notion… ✻ A browser window will open for authentication If your browser doesn't open automatically, copy this URL manually (c to copy) https://mcp.notion.com/authorize?response_type=code&client_id=... If the redirect page shows a connection error, paste the URL from your browser's address bar: URL > http://localhost:3118/callback?code=... If, like me, you're running Claude Code on a remote host over SSH, that last URL > line is what you need. After you approve, Notion redirects you to http://localhost:3118/callback?code=..., but that localhost is the machine your browser is on, not the remote box where Claude Code is waiting for the callback, and I hadn't forwarded port 3118 over SSH, so the page just shows a connection error. Copy that full URL from your browser's address bar and paste it into the console's URL > prompt to hand the code back to the remote. Running Claude Code locally, you won't hit this; the browser loops back on its own.
When you approve in the browser, it lets you pick which pages to expose. This is where you control what it can see. Tick only what you want to grant. It can't touch the rest.
Step 3: Confirm the connection After authorizing, the terminal returns:
1 2 /mcp ⎿ Authentication successful. Connected to notion. Seeing Connected to notion means it worked, and every time you open Claude Code from now on it reconnects automatically, and you never manually launch anything. To revoke access, disconnect notion under /mcp.
Connecting Notion MCP in Codex, Claude Desktop, and Antigravity In one line: under the hood they all connect to Notion's hosted MCP, all authorize over OAuth, and all auto-load after setup. The only difference is whether you add it with a command, a small config block, or a click in a menu, and none of them need an extra package.
Tool How you add it Authorize Claude Code one claude mcp add command /mcp, browser opens Codex CLI (ChatGPT) add a notion block to ~/.codex/config.toml codex mcp login notion, browser opens Claude Desktop Settings → Connectors, search for notion and add it, no URL, account-bound browser opens on the spot Antigravity add a notion block to ~/.gemini/config/mcp_config.json reload, browser opens Codex CLI (the terminal version of ChatGPT) does have a codex mcp add command, but it only takes local stdio servers (a launch command after --), so Notion's remote URL doesn't fit it. For a remote server the official way is to edit ~/.codex/config.toml and add this:
1 2 [mcp_servers.notion] url = "https://mcp.notion.com/mcp" Save, then run codex mcp login notion for the same browser authorization. (Some Codex versions treat remote MCP as experimental, so if it won't connect, add a [features] block with experimental_use_rmcp_client = true in config.toml and try again.)
Claude Desktop is even less work: no config file, no URL to paste. Go to Settings → Connectors, search for notion, click to add it, and complete the OAuth flow right there (this feature is Pro/Max/Team/Enterprise only).
A Claude Desktop connector, though, is tied to your Claude account and syncs to every device you log in on (web and mobile included), unlike Claude Code and Codex, where it lives only in a local config file. That means anyone logged into that account can read your Notion through it. So if you share your Claude account with family, don't connect it here. Use the Claude Code approach above, which stays on your machine.
Antigravity (Google's Gemini agentic IDE, which I covered in Antigravity vs. GitHub Copilot) keeps its config at ~/.gemini/config/mcp_config.json (shared by the IDE and CLI). Add a server pointed at the URL:
1 2 3 4 5 6 7 { "mcpServers": { "notion": { "serverUrl": "https://mcp.notion.com/mcp" } } } Paste it in, reload, and authorize in the browser the same way. In the UI you can find the button to open this file under Settings → Customizations.
Connect Notion with a personal access token (PAT) If your case is headless automation, or you want the server itself running on your own machine with access scoped to a single page, Notion also offers a static personal access token (PAT): on the developer page, create a connection with Access token as the authorization type and you'll get a key starting with ntn_.... Then add the local Notion MCP server in Claude Code with that key:
1 claude mcp add notion -e NOTION_TOKEN=ntn_your_token -- npx -y @notionhq/notion-mcp-server The @notionhq/notion-mcp-server there runs locally on your machine. Notion now actively maintains only the remote hosted MCP, and this local repo sees little upkeep, so I'd still reach for the OAuth route above first.
Conclusion Connecting Notion to an AI tool isn't that hard: add one config line, authorize in the browser, and it connects, with no server to host and no extra packages. The tools differ only in how you add it. Underneath they all connect to Notion's official MCP. Once it's wired up, you can have Claude or Codex write Notion notes straight from the CLI, or analyze a PDF locally and drop the results right into Notion. I find it genuinely handy.
The real reason to connect this way instead of the web version's one-click is still privacy: with a tool like Claude Code that keeps the authorization in a local config, you pick the pages yourself and, even on a shared account, only you can reach it (Claude Desktop is the exception: it binds to your account, so don't use it on a shared one). So if privacy matters, I'd connect MCP locally wherever you can. And Notion isn't the only MCP worth running locally: for development there are plenty more, like Context7, Playwright MCP, Chrome DevTools MCP, and GitHub's MCP server. Wiring several of them up locally lets Claude or Codex reach more tools and pull more precise information, doing more in one pass.
References Get started with MCP—Notion Developers Connect Claude Code to tools via MCP—Claude Code Docs Authorization—Notion Docs Model Context Protocol in Codex—OpenAI Developers Model Context Protocol—Google Antigravity Documentation
title: Add Notion MCP Locally: Three Steps for Claude Code, Codex, and Antigravity

Why Building Your Own AI Agent Is So Hard Say you want a little helper that fetches the latest from a fixed handful of websites every day and pulls it into a single summary for you. Even for a chore this small—fixed sources, on a schedule—the mainstream way to build your own AI Agent goes roughly like this: get a computer, install something like OpenClaw, and follow a long tutorial through a series of setup steps. Just getting the environment up and running, on top of a dense wall of details, already trips up a lot of people.
Then you have to pick a model, and whichever route you take has its own barrier.
Going local: the model weights have to fit entirely into memory to run (on a typical PC it's mostly your GPU's VRAM; on Apple Silicon that's unified memory). Entry level is roughly 12–16GB to run 7B–14B small models. But models that size have clear weaknesses: weaker answers, more mistakes, and they often can't keep up with anything complex. For something genuinely usable you generally need a 30B-class model, whose Q4-quantized weights alone run 22–24GB, which works out to 24–32GB of memory or more. That means buying a not-cheap machine first.
Going cloud: from the start, you have to add a credit card and start counting token usage.
So it becomes: before I've actually done anything, just the getting-ready step already means either spending money on hardware or getting billed the moment I add a card. That barrier alone, I think, makes a lot of people give up.
On top of that, the tutorials for these tools are mostly in English. The web looks full of them, but very few setups keep running reliably over time. It's common to get halfway through and find the versions don't match, or the service was shut down ages ago.
What's worse, the whole AI ecosystem iterates so fast that packages update every other day, and just keeping up with the upgrades is tiring on its own. The flip side of fast iteration is that security risk comes with it: these projects, along with their long chain of dependencies, regularly turn up CVE vulnerabilities. Self-hosting an agent means chasing new features and patching security holes at the same time, and the long-term maintenance cost is far higher than it first looks.
Most of What We Do Is Just a Fixed Workflow But think about it: a lot of what we do on a computer every day is actually a fixed set of steps, the kind of thing you could line up in advance, like Shortcuts on iOS.
Lock down the mechanical parts of a flow (fetching data, moving files, sending messages) as fixed steps, and only hand the small part that genuinely needs understanding or judgment to an LLM. That buys you two things: the whole thing runs faster, and token usage drops a lot, because you're not asking the AI to figure out everything from scratch, just calling on it at the key moments.
There's also a more important property this buys you: predictability. If you let the AI decide every step from start to finish, the results tend to be unstable. It does it one way today and another way tomorrow. But put the LLM inside a fixed flow you've laid out in advance, where it only handles the one bounded judgment you've assigned it and the inputs and outputs around it stay under your control, and the result comes out consistent every time.
That's the direction Yobi is built in. The goal is to let you spin up your own simple AI Agent with the least effort possible, and hand off the small, repetitive, fixed tasks in your day to it.
What Is Yobi Yobi is a local-first, open-source (MIT) AI automation desktop app for Windows and macOS.
The way it works is simple. Yobi has a built-in browser window, opens up the web pages for ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, and Duck.ai, types your prompt into the page, and reads the response back, the same way you'd use the site yourself. It doesn't call the providers' official APIs, and it doesn't run any AI model on your machine. For the ones that need an account, it reuses the session you're already logged into in your browser; some, like Gemini and Duck.ai, work out of the box with no login at all. (If you happen to have an API key already, there's an optional BYOK mode in settings that will use it, but that's a side option. The browser is still the default.)
Because it goes through each provider's own web page rather than a paid API, there's no API key to set up and no card to add, and it skips the hardware barrier of running a local model, too.
Open Yobi and you get a chat window like most other AI services, so pick a provider, type, and you're chatting.
Automating these web interfaces is against the providers' terms of service. Yobi doesn't bypass any technical protections: no CAPTCHA solving, no rate-limit evasion, and no IP rotation. With normal, light personal use, the most you're likely to hit is the occasional "verify you are human" prompt that you clear by hand. Heavy or abusive automation is what tends to get blocked. Use Yobi responsibly, and don't use it for anything illegal.
It's built for your own computer. The machine you work on, or a home PC that stays on 24/7, is a great fit for leaving it running, and it's all GUI, no command line at any point.
Download and Install Yobi Windows: installing from the Microsoft Store is the easiest route. It updates itself and won't trip the unsigned-app warning. If you'd rather install by hand, the Releases page has an x64 installer. It isn't code-signed yet, so Windows throws up a protection screen the first time: click More info → Run anyway to continue.
macOS: grab the .dmg from Releases, the one with arm64 in its name for M1/M2/M3/M4 chips, x64 for Intel. Not sure which Mac you have? Click the Apple menu (top-left) → About This Mac and look at the Chip / Processor line. Open the .dmg and drag Yobi into your Applications folder. That's it installed.
macOS blocking it on first launch is normal. The app isn't signed with Apple's (paid) certificate yet, so the first time you open it macOS says "can't be opened because it is from an unidentified developer." It's not malware—it's just Apple's default guard. Pick one way around it:
Easier: double-click Yobi once (it gets blocked), then go to System Settings → Privacy & Security, scroll down to the blocked Yobi, and click Open Anyway. One-and-done (if you're comfortable with the terminal): open Terminal, paste this line and press Enter (it'll ask for your login password—it's normal that nothing appears as you type): 1 sudo xattr -rd com.apple.quarantine /Applications/Yobi.app Most people just need the prebuilt package. No need to build it yourself. If you want to tinker with the source or run the latest dev build, the GitHub project page has full build instructions.
Install it, open it, and you can start chatting right away. Let's walk through the basic features most people use day to day first, then move on to the more advanced Telegram integration.
Yobi's Everyday Features Send selected text to AI with one key This is Yobi's core. Select some text in any app → press Alt+G → it's auto-sent into the chat window → the response is saved straight to a timestamped Markdown file, without you lifting a finger. Translating, summarizing, rewriting, drafting a commit message. These "give it a chunk of text, get a chunk back" chores are exactly what it's for.
Tip: to keep the hotkey responsive at all times, let Yobi sit in the background via Settings → General → System Tray. If you don't like Alt+G, change it in Settings → General → Hotkey (the macOS default is Command+G).
Switch between providers anytime All four providers are in the same window. Whichever one is better at a given kind of question, just switch to it, no need to keep a pile of tabs open.
Responses auto-save to Markdown Every response is automatically saved as Markdown with a timestamp. No more "that answer was great, but I closed the window and now it's gone." (Markdown is a plain-text note format with the .md extension. You can open it in Notepad. The files are saved in Yobi's folder by default, and you can view or change the path in settings.)
And for the times you'd rather leave no trace, Ctrl+Shift+I switches to temporary chat mode, where replies are never written to disk.
Export as an image or PDF Want to share a response or save it as something nicer? Export it directly as PNG, WebP, or PDF. Gradient palette, layout direction, whether to show the original prompt, the provider name, and the timestamp: all adjustable.
Customize tone and prompt preferences Tacking "please answer in Traditional Chinese and keep it brief" onto every question gets tiring, so Yobi makes it a setting: tone (Default / Professional / Casual / Direct), length (Auto / Concise / Detailed), and a block of custom instructions prepended to every prompt automatically. You can also save your go-to phrasings as reusable templates.
Flows: Chain Fixed Steps Into Your Own Little Agent Everything above is press-once, do-one-thing. A flow chains several steps into something that runs itself to the end: just like the iOS Shortcuts idea from earlier, no coding, just drag-and-drop. This is the core of how Yobi lets you build your own Agent.
A flow has three parts: when it triggers, what it does in between, and where the result goes.
There are five triggers, and one flow can use several at once:
Trigger Description ⌨️ Hotkey A dedicated global shortcut for this flow ⏰ Scheduled Runs daily / weekly. Set the time and it fires automatically 🤖 Bot command A custom Telegram or LINE command, e.g. /news <keyword> 💬 Chat command Type /your-command right in Yobi's chat box 👆 Manual Press run yourself whenever you need it There are 44 skills to use in between, with more being added. Roughly, they fall into these groups:
Group What it covers 📥 Pull data Web pages, RSS, HTTP APIs, YouTube transcripts, even live stock / forex / weather, no key needed 🌐 Drive a browser Open tabs, click, fill forms, take screenshots 🧠 Ask AI ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Duck.ai, or your own API key via BYOK 📤 Send results Telegram or LINE, email, a file, or the clipboard 🛠️ Run anything Programs, JavaScript, shell commands, plus system and power controls 🔀 Control flow Loops, conditions, scheduling Never built an automation before? You don't have to. Describe what you want in plain language, like "every weekday at 8am, summarize my RSS feed and send it to Telegram", and AI assembles the whole flow for you. Tweak any step afterwards.
Each step writes its result to a named variable, and later steps pull it in with {{variable_name}}. To take the classic example, chaining "fetch RSS → summarize with AI → push to Telegram" looks roughly like this:
1 2 3 4 5 6 7 RSS Feed → a list of {title, link} for new articles → output: articles Stop Flow → end here if the list is empty For each → each item is called article Fetch page → open {{article.link}} and read the body → output: page LLM prompt → "Summarize this in three sentences: {{page}}" → output: summary Telegram → message: {{article.title}} plus {{summary}} End Loop Pair that flow with the Scheduled trigger and it becomes: every morning it fetches the tech news I subscribe to, summarizes it into three sentences with AI, and pushes it to the Telegram on my phone. I'm still asleep and the summary is already in my chat. The key part is that fetching and sending are all fixed steps, and the AI only handles the small summarize bit in the middle, so it runs fast, saves tokens, and gives you a stable result every day.
Don't want to start from an empty canvas? The template gallery has 12 ready-made flows to drop in: RSS summary pushes, web monitoring (watch a site for new content, analyze it with AI, then push it out), YouTube subscription digests (summarize new videos from the channels you follow, thumbnails included). Pick one and a setup wizard walks you through the fields it needs, so you're not digging through every step yourself. Flows can be exported as .json files to share, or imported from a file or URL.
Controlling Yobi Remotely with a Telegram or LINE Bot Yobi hooks up to both Telegram and LINE, so even when you're away from your computer, you can tell it to do things from your phone. The two are equivalent: they share the same command settings, and a flow's bot triggers and push steps work across either. Telegram is the walkthrough below; for LINE, settings has a two-step webhook guide that gets you there.
Roughly three steps:
Get a Bot Token: search for @BotFather on Telegram and start it, tap Open to begin the chat, pick Create a New Bot, and follow the prompt to enter a bot name. It's straightforward and you'll be done in under three minutes, and at the end it hands you a Bot Token (i.e. an API key). If you'd rather watch it done, this video walks through the whole thing: How To Create A Telegram Bot In Python For Beginners (the bot-creation and token part near the start is all you need—you can skip the Python code after). Paste the token and enable it: go to Settings → Bots, paste the token into the Telegram Bot field, and hit Update Token. Once it's enabled, the Runtime Status below turns a green Running, meaning the bot is live. Generate a pairing code and invite the people you trust: in the Pairing section on the same page, hit Generate Code to get a pairing code and hand it to someone you trust. They DM your bot on Telegram and send /start <code> (or just tap the pairing link) to finish pairing. Only paired people can drive the bot, so you can safely share it with family or coworkers to use together. Once paired, these built-in commands are available anytime:
Command Description /gpt, /gemini, /pplx, /duck + a prompt Send it to that provider (command names are yours to change) /output <mode> Set the reply format (md / png / webp / pdf) /status Check the current status /restart Restart Yobi Out with only your phone? Sending /gpt translate this into Japanese is all it takes. And if you'd rather not type commands at all, you can set it up so plain messages get answered as they come.
Hooking a bot up to an AI so it answers one message at a time is handy, but it's really closer to moving the chat onto your phone, not quite an agent yet. What gives it the shape of one is pairing it with the Bot command trigger from earlier: the same message can kick off a whole pre-arranged flow that fetches, decides, and outputs in one go. Getting a task actually carried out from start to finish. That's the part Yobi is really after.
Settings and Privacy A quick pass over settings, mostly options to make it more comfortable: themes (including one that follows your system's light/dark mode), reading layout, response timeout, launch at startup, minimize to tray on close, Markdown zoom, and separate notification toggles for completion, success, and failure. Settings and data can be backed up in full and restored on another machine, and the interface supports 9 languages.
There's also a usage page with run counts, success rate, and a 14-day trend chart, all computed locally, so you can see at a glance whether your flows are actually running clean.
Two more are worth calling out. Email (SMTP) lets a flow mail its results straight to you, since not everyone wants everything landing in Telegram or LINE. And BYOK: if you already hold an OpenAI-compatible key (OpenAI, OpenRouter, Together, Groq, a local server—they all count) or a Gemini key, you can add it as an extra provider and pick it in chat and in flows like any other. The browser stays the default; this is just one more option.
On privacy, the key points: Yobi does no telemetry and collects none of your usage behavior, and all automation logic and stats run on your own machine. Your bot tokens, SMTP password, and BYOK keys are handed to the OS's built-in encrypted vault (Credential Manager on Windows, Keychain on macOS) and encrypted before being written to disk. What you ask the AI goes to the relevant provider and is subject to each one's privacy policy, and those platforms are outside the author's control. The whole project is open source, so all the logic is right there on GitHub for you to check.
Conclusion The whole reason I made Yobi was to lower the barrier to building your own AI Agent as much as possible. No dropping a pile of money on a machine that can run a big model, and no adding a card to get billed from day one: just connect the web interfaces you're already logged into, line up your fixed steps as a flow, and the small chores in your day can run themselves. And because the AI is only called inside a fixed flow, the result is predictable. It won't work fine today and suddenly go sideways tomorrow.
Yobi isn't trying to replace full platforms like OpenClaw or n8n either. What it's after is letting you get simple automation plus an LLM working with the resources you already have.
If you come up with other applications, or have any suggestions for Yobi, you're welcome to open an Issue on GitHub and discuss it. If you want to tinker or are curious what it's built on, the source is all there too.
And if Yobi helps you out and you'd like to support me in keeping it going, you can buy me a coffee on the sponsor page, or just drop a ⭐ on the project on GitHub. Both help more people find it, and keep me motivated to keep it updated.
References Telegram Bots—official documentation
title: Yobi: AI Automation That Drives ChatGPT & Gemini Through Their Web Interfaces to Build Your Own Agent

Introduction I've always admired the polish of Apple's HomeKit ecosystem. With a HomePod mini in the house, whether I'm streaming music or controlling natively supported smart accessories, the response time and stability have both kept me happy.
But the cracks show fast.
A few of my TP-Link smart plugs don't support HomeKit. Meaning I have to open a separate app just to toggle them. My old infrared air conditioner is stuck in its own app. The Android TV box in the living room can't even be turned on remotely. Three different apps for three devices in the same room.
At some point I got fed up and used some spare time to set up Home Assistant (HA) and see if I could fix this.
How Smart Homes Work: Why We Need Home Assistant The short version: your phone speaks Wi-Fi, but a bunch of smart home devices don't. Why? Battery life.
Devices plugged into the wall—like smart plugs or light bulbs—can afford the power draw of Wi-Fi. But a battery-powered door sensor or wireless switch running on a coin cell? Wi-Fi would kill the battery in days. That's why most of these smaller gadgets run on:
Zigbee: Extremely low-power, short-range, good for sensors and switches. Thread: Similar idea but newer. It's the standard Apple and Google have been pushing. Devices can also relay signals through each other like a mesh, which helps range. Your router doesn't speak either of those protocols. So your network needs a physical bridge (gateway): a device that stays powered on and translates between the low-power radio signals and your local network.
Big Tech's Walled Gardens and the Reality of Matter To lock you into their ecosystems, major brands traditionally required you to buy their specific proprietary hubs. If a device didn't natively support HomeKit, it remained trapped inside its own app unless you bought yet another bridge.
The industry tried to fix this with the Matter protocol, a universal standard backed by Apple, Google, Amazon, and others. On paper, Matter means one device works everywhere. In practice, it's been a slow rollout. Brands like Philips Hue and IKEA have been dragging their feet on full support, and older hardware either needs firmware updates or just won't qualify at all. You still end up buying proprietary hubs if you want everything to work together.
Home Assistant is where I landed instead. It connects to basically anything—official brand hubs, direct USB radio dongles, local network APIs—and pulls it all into one dashboard. Getting my Synology NAS stats in there was as simple as searching for the integration and entering the IP and credentials.
A Low-Cost, 24/7 Solution Since HA needs to run 24/7, the question is what machine it runs on.
A dedicated HA mini PC runs around TWD 3,000. My desktop already stays on all the time as a local server, so I just carved out a small chunk of resources and ran HA inside a Windows Hyper-V virtual machine. Zero extra cost.
One thing worth knowing: if you want remote control via the Apple Home app when you're away from home, you still need a HomePod mini or Apple TV on your network. HA handles the local translation of non-certified devices, but Apple's infrastructure is what actually bridges the gap to your phone on cellular. That's just how HomeKit works, HA or not.
If you don't care about Apple Home and want to use the native HA app for remote access, you'll need to handle that yourself. Don't just open a port on your router. That's asking for trouble. The cleaner option is Tailscale. Install the Tailscale add-on in HA, and you get an encrypted VPN tunnel between your phone and the VM without touching your router config. When you're out, turn on Tailscale and HA is right there.
Here's how I set the whole thing up, from VM creation to getting AdGuard Home and NAS monitoring showing up in iOS.
Four Steps to Setting Up Home Assistant on Hyper-V If this is your first time using a VM, here's the full process:
Step 1: Prerequisites and Downloading Files Enable Hyper-V: Turn on the Hyper-V virtualization feature in Windows 10/11 (Pro or Enterprise). Download the Image: Head to the Official Home Assistant Installation Page, download the Hyper-V (.vhdx) file, and extract it. Set the Storage Path: Move the .vhdx file to a permanent directory (e.g., C:\Users\wells\HomeAssistant). Do not move or delete this file later, or your virtual machine will fail to boot and cause data loss. Step 2: Create an "External Virtual Switch" This is what gets the virtual machine an IP on the same subnet as your router (e.g., 192.168.x.x), so it can talk directly to the other smart devices on your network.
Open Hyper-V Manager and select Virtual Switch Manager from the Actions panel on the right. Select New virtual network switch -> choose External -> click Create Virtual Switch. Configure the Properties: Name: Enter HA-External-Switch. Connection type: Select External network and use the dropdown to choose the network adapter your computer currently uses for internet access. Crucial Checkbox: Check Allow management operating system to share this network adapter, or your host Windows machine loses its internet connection. Click OK. If a warning pops up regarding temporary network disruption, click Yes. Step 3: Create the Virtual Machine and Optimize Performance This step deploys the virtual machine with "Quick Create" and sorts out its resource allocation in one go.
Click Quick Create on the right side of the Hyper-V Manager:
Select an image: Choose Local installation source and browse to the .vhdx file you prepared in Step 1. Advanced settings: Click More options in the bottom right, name the VM HA or Home Assistant, and set the network to the HA-External-Switch created in Step 2. Security: You must uncheck "Enable Windows Secure Boot." Click Create Virtual Machine. Once created, do not connect to it just yet. Click Edit Settings in the confirmation window and adjust the resources:
Memory: Set it to 4096 MB (4 GB) and uncheck "Enable Dynamic Memory" to prevent resource contention. Processor: Set the number of virtual processors to 2. Click Apply and OK to save your changes.
Step 4: Boot the Virtual Machine and Initialize the System With the resources set, it's time to fire up Home Assistant OS.
Back in the main Hyper-V Manager interface, right-click your newly created VM and select Connect. In the console window that pops up, click Start.
A stream of boot logs will scroll past as the Linux subsystem initializes. Wait about 1 to 3 minutes. When the welcome banner appears, your system is officially live on your local network:
Open a web browser on any device connected to the same local network and navigate to: http://homeassistant.local:8123 (or use the explicit IP shown on screen, e.g., http://192.168.1.125:8123).
The system will download core components in the background. Once the onboarding screen appears, follow the prompts to create your admin account and set your location. That completes the Hyper-V side of the setup.
Device Integration: Adding Hardware to Your Dashboard With the system up, next is adding devices to the Home Assistant dashboard.
Click the + icon in the top right corner of the web UI and select Add Device.
To integrate an AdGuard Home instance, type adguard into the search bar. Select the integration, enter your host IP/URL, port, and admin credentials. Once submitted, your AdGuard ad-blocking toggles and real-time statistics will populate right into HA.
The same approach works for Synology DSM. Enter your NAS's local IP and credentials, and HA pulls the server's hardware status and system metrics in automatically.
Syncing HA Devices to Apple Home Getting your HA devices into Apple Home is actually pretty easy. Two things: set up a bridge in HA, then scan a QR code with your iPhone.
Create a HomeKit Bridge in HA Click the + icon in the top right of HA (Add Device), search for apple, and select Apple. Choose HomeKit Bridge. In the configuration window, check the device domains you want to expose to Apple (such as Switch or Sensor) and hit submit. (Note: Media players and TVs will automatically be isolated into "accessory mode" so they get dedicated control interfaces within iOS). iPhone QR Code Pairing Once the bridge is created, click the Notifications (bell icon) in the bottom-left corner of HA. You will see a dedicated setup QR code alongside an 8-digit PIN (standalone accessories like TVs will also be displayed separately here). Open the Home app on your iPhone, tap the + icon in the top right, select Add Accessory, and scan the QR code off your screen. When the prompt detects the bridge, tap Add to Home and assign your devices to their respective rooms. Once paired, look at your iOS Home app. Peripherals that previously locked you out of HomeKit—like your TV or AdGuard switches—are all in place. Siri voice commands, automation triggers, or checking the NAS drive temperature from an Apple Watch all work from there. (Note: The Home app UI only showcases the AdGuard Home switch controlled via HA).
Conclusion After setting up the HomeKit Bridge, I can now pull most of my non-HomeKit hardware into the Apple Home app without buying new devices.
Before HA, buying smart home gear meant filtering for that "Works with Apple HomeKit" badge, which pretty much always comes with a price premium. Now I just check if something has a Home Assistant integration. That's a way broader pool of hardware, and a lot of it is cheaper. My IR-controlled appliances that were trapped in proprietary apps are now controllable through Apple Home.
For new purchases, I still lean toward devices that natively support Matter: it's the least-headache option long term and works across both iOS and Android without needing HA in the loop. But for everything already sitting in my home, HA bridged the gap pretty cleanly.
References Windows - Home Assistant HomeKit Bridge - Home Assistant Matter Smart Home Systems - IKEA Philips Hue and Matter | Philips Hue hassio-addons/app-tailscale: Tailscale
title: Hyper-V Home Assistant Setup: Easily Bridge Non-Certified Devices to HomeKit

Introduction Since its debut at CES 2026 earlier this year, the Aqara U400 has been high on my smart home watchlist. While my current place didn't have an urgent need for a lock upgrade, my long-standing interest in Ultra-Wideband (UWB) technology—and a recent stroke of luck—finally landed a unit in my hands.
This is a straightforward unboxing, plus a look at how UWB fixes the security and precision problems of Bluetooth unlocking.
Why Do We Need UWB Technology? Ultra-Wideband (UWB) isn't exactly a new buzzword. Apple brought it into the mainstream back in 2019 with the U1 chip in the iPhone 11. However, it's only now, in 2026, that we're seeing its killer app potential fully realized in the smart lock industry.
Smart Lock Evolution Comparison Type Core Technology Usage Pros Limitations Traditional Tag / RFID RFID / NFC Physical card or fob Low cost, widely used Easy to lose; locked out if forgotten Biometric Locks Fingerprint / Face / Vein Active touch or scanning Keyless, high security Difficult to use when carrying groceries Mobile Proximity NFC (e.g., Apple Home Key) Tap phone to lock Digital wallet experience Still requires taking the phone out UWB Hands-Free UWB + ToF Ranging Automatic proximity detection High-precision; true hands-free experience Ecosystem still maturing Solving the Bluetooth Problem In the past, many smart locks attempted "auto-unlock" using Bluetooth, but the experience was notoriously hit-or-miss. Bluetooth relies on Received Signal Strength Indicator (RSSI) to guess distance, which is easily interfered with by walls or the human body. This led to awkward scenarios: sometimes the door would unlock while you were still waiting for the elevator; other times, you'd be standing right in front of the door with zero response.
UWB uses Time of Flight (ToF), which works like radar, to calculate the exact time it takes for a signal to travel back and forth. This allows the lock to know your absolute distance and whether you are actually approaching the door. This precision is what makes hands-free unlocking finally feel reliable.
Beyond accuracy, UWB offers two major advantages in security and spatial awareness:
Relay Attack Prevention: UWB uses STS (Scrambled Timestamp Sequence) technology. Even if someone tries to intercept and relay your signal to spoof your location, faking the timing is close to impossible, which is what matters for residential security. Indoor vs. Outdoor Detection: This is perhaps the most practical feature. By combining UWB with Angle of Arrival (AoA) algorithms, the lock doesn't just know how far away you are; it knows your direction. It can distinguish between you walking around your living room and you approaching from the outside, effectively ending the annoyance of the door accidentally unlocking while you're just walking past it inside. Note: We are starting to see products supporting Bluetooth 6.0 Channel Sounding in 2026. While this tech also aims to improve ranging, UWB currently maintains a clear lead in positioning accuracy, interference resistance, and overall ecosystem maturity.
Prerequisites and Limitations Adopting new tech does come with a few caveats:
Heavy Apple Ecosystem Reliance: Currently, the hands-free experience is essentially tailor-made for Apple users. You'll need an iPhone 11 or later, or an Apple Watch Series 6 or later. Crucially, you need a Thread-enabled hub (like a HomePod or Apple TV) before the response feels instant. Double-Door Configurations (Taiwan Context): Many apartments in Taiwan feature a "foyer gate + main inner door" setup. If you install the U400 on the outer gate, I highly recommend enabling "Dual Door Mode" in the Aqara Home App and refining the "Approach Direction" settings. This prevents the lock from constantly cycling if you're just pausing in the foyer to change shoes. Hardware Unboxing & Specs Packaging and Accessories The Aqara U400 box highlights support for multiple protocols, so it works with almost every major hub on the market.
Key features on the box include:
Matter: This is what gives it cross-platform compatibility. Whether you use Apple Home, Google Home, Amazon Alexa, Samsung SmartThings, or Home Assistant, it connects directly without being locked into one ecosystem. Thread: Compared to traditional Bluetooth or Wi-Fi, Thread offers faster response times, lower power consumption, and a more stable mesh network for local automation. Inside the box, you'll find the interior and exterior assemblies, latch hardware, mounting screws, a USB-C rechargeable lithium battery, an M100 Thread hub (included in some kits), and a paper template for precise installation.
Lock Body Durability and Power Management Design The image below clearly shows the internal structure of the Aqara U400's front and rear panels. The exterior panel on the left features a connecting cable and the spindle, the core mechanical component that drives the rotation of the latch. Meanwhile, the interior panel on the right houses the batteries, supplying power to the exterior side via a ribbon cable.
During actual installation, the spindle passes through the square hole of the latch, and screws are then used to tightly secure both the interior and exterior panels to the door. When the motor activates or the knob is manually turned, the spindle engages the latch to complete the locking and unlocking actions.
Installation & Setup Tips While the U400 is marketed as a sandwich-style installation that fits standard deadbolt holes without extra drilling, every door is different. Check your specs before you remove your old lock. Also, if your old hardware has been there for years, a can of WD-40 helps with the seized screws.
Door Measurements Before starting, verify these dimensions:
Door Thickness: Ideally between 35mm and 55mm. Bore Hole Diameter: If your current hole is only 38mm, the official recommendation is to expand it to 54mm so the wiring and the install have room. Handing: The U400 is universal (supports left/right and inward/outward swings). Backset: The distance from the door edge to the center of the handle hole. Use the included paper template to verify this instantly. Critical Step: Latch Calibration Once the hardware is powered up, the most important part of the app setup is Calibration. The motor will extend and retract the deadbolt automatically. This isn't just a test; it's the system learning the physical limits of your door frame:
Finding the Limits: The system needs to know exactly how deep the bolt goes to be "Locked" and how far it must retract to be "Unlocked." This minimizes mechanical wear and keeps the motor from overworking itself. Auto-Lock Reliability: Without accurate calibration, the auto-lock might fail to engage fully or, conversely, exert too much pressure on the frame, leading to battery drain or false alarms. Software Integration For this initial test, I used the included Aqara M100 gateway as the Thread Border Router. If you're setting this up permanently, a HomePod or Apple TV is what gets you the instant response time.
Out of the box, my unit was on version 3.1.0.0, and the Home app immediately prompted a firmware update. Do the update. It includes the groundwork for Aliro, the upcoming cross-platform UWB standard that will eventually allow Android phones to enjoy the same hands-free experience currently exclusive to Apple.
Multiple Ways to Unlock The Aqara U400 offers 9 different ways to get inside. This makes it friendly for everyone from tech-enthusiasts to grandparents who prefer traditional methods.
Two standout software features:
Phantom Passwords: To stop onlookers from reading your code, you can type up to 20 digits of random numbers, as long as your actual 6-digit code is hidden somewhere within that string. Scheduled Access: Useful for cleaning services or temporary guests. You can issue "One-time passwords" or codes that only work during specific windows (e.g., Wednesdays from 2 PM to 4 PM), so access rights can be sliced quite finely. Is it worth it for Android users? To be objective: Android users currently miss out on UWB hands-free unlocking. The fingerprint and NFC experience, though, is already solid. Since the hardware already includes the UWB chip and Matter over Thread, the parts for what comes next are already in the box. Once the Aliro protocol is fully integrated into the Android ecosystem, a simple software update should unlock the full feature set.
Conclusion The Aqara U400 does more than get rid of your keys. With UWB added, it can tell that you are walking toward the door rather than just standing near it.
While the Android ecosystem still needs time for UWB and Aliro support to fully mature, if you're already an Apple user, this lock has no real competitor right now.
Comparing it to established brands in the Taiwan market—such as Samsung, Philips, or Yale—you'd typically need a budget of over TWD 20,000 to find hardware with similar specs, and even then, they often lack UWB or Apple Home Key support. By contrast, the U400 is currently available on Amazon for roughly TWD 8,500. Even factoring in international shipping, the total cost stays well under the TWD 10,000 mark.
If you're in the market for a new lock and want to cover everything in one go, the Aqara U400 is worth buying now.
References Aqara Smart Lock U400 User Manual Aqara Smart Lock U400 FAQ: Installation, Features, and Troubleshooting
title: Unboxing the Aqara U400: The New Gold Standard for UWB Smart Locks

Introduction It's been almost a year since we published Boosting Coding Efficiency and Developer Experience with GitHub Copilot Agent Mode. Over the past year, the pace of GitHub's policy changes and AI model updates has been so blistering that it's honestly hard to keep up.
Looking back at April 2025, we were still thrilled about VS Code officially launching Agent Mode and exploring how to integrate it with the Model Context Protocol (MCP). By 2026, with the user base growing and long-running Agent Mode sessions becoming normal, GitHub has been making move after move to reflect true operational costs.
In March and April 2026, GitHub first revoked the ability for Student accounts to manually select high-tier models. They then introduced strict Session Limits and Weekly Limits for Individual plans. On April 10, GitHub officially suspended all new Copilot Pro trials. By April 20, they stopped accepting new subscriptions for the Individual plan altogether, leaving new users with only Copilot Free. GitHub's stated reason was abuse of the trial system, a decision made to protect platform integrity and the experience of existing paying developers.
The biggest shakeup arrives on June 1, 2026, when Copilot fully transitions to AI Credits. This isn't just a rebranding, it's a fundamental overhaul from a per-request model to volume-based token billing.
Billing Reform & Plan Breakdown Why the Switch to AI Credits? The core driver behind this overhaul is the widespread adoption of Agent Mode.
Under the 2025 Premium Request Units (PRU) system, it cost the same number of points whether you asked for simple syntax help or had the AI spend minutes refactoring thousands of lines of code. But long-context conversations and cross-file agent operations chew through huge amounts of tokens. The old model couldn't carry the inference costs anymore, so GitHub moved to pay-as-you-go billing based on actual token usage.
New Plans and Migration Need-to-Knows Starting June 1, while the monthly fees will stay the same, the included quotas will transition from PRUs to their equivalent value in AI Credits.
Plan Monthly Fee Legacy PRU Quota Post-June AI Credits Notes Copilot Free USD 0 50 PRU/mo Limited Free Tier Best for light queries Copilot Pro USD 10 300 PRU/mo 1,000 Credits Equivalent to USD 10 Copilot Pro+ USD 39 1,500 PRU/mo 3,900 Credits Equivalent to USD 39 Copilot Business USD 19/user 300 PRU/mo 1,900 Credits* 3,000 Credits during promo Copilot Enterprise USD 39/user 1,000 PRU/mo 3,900 Credits* 7,000 Credits during promo Note on Enterprise Plans: AI Credits are pooled at the billing entity level (e.g., 100 Business users share 190,000 Credits, rather than having 100 isolated accounts). There is a promotional quota allowance for the first three months (June to August), after which limits will revert to the standard amount.
Model Multiplier Changes for Annual Subscribers For individual users who locked in an annual plan before June 1, you'll stay on the PRU billing method, but new multipliers will be enforced to reflect the higher inference costs. According to GitHub's docs, here is what to expect:
Model Old Multiplier New Multiplier Details Claude Sonnet 4.5/4.6 1 6–9 Cost jumps 6–9x Claude Opus 4.6/4.7 3–7.5 27 Cost jumps up to 27x GPT-5.4/5.5 1 6+ At least 6x for high-tier models GPT-5 mini 0 0.33 Previously free, now costs 0.33x For example: If you were previously getting around 300 effective uses of Claude Sonnet 4.6 per month, that drops to roughly 33–50 uses, a 6 to 9 times cost increase.
Annual subscribers keep paying in PRUs until their current plan expires, but it's worth evaluating a monthly plan or other options before renewal.
Model Rates & Selection Strategy The baseline metric is 1 AI Credit = USD 0.01. Picking a model is now like ordering off a menu. Below is the estimated cost per million tokens (in USD):
Provider / Model Input Cached Output Notes OpenAI Series GPT-4.1 $2.00 $0.50 $8.00 Lightweight general purpose GPT-5 mini $0.25 $0.025 $2.00 Ultra-lightweight GPT-5.2 $1.75 $0.175 $14.00 General purpose GPT-5.2-Codex $1.75 $0.175 $14.00 Code specialized GPT-5.4 $2.50 $0.25 $15.00 General purpose GPT-5.4 mini $0.75 $0.075 $4.50 Fast & lightweight GPT-5.4 nano $0.20 $0.02 $1.25 Featherweight GPT-5.5 $5.00 $0.50 $30.00 Advanced reasoning Anthropic Series Claude Haiku 4.5 $1.00 $0.10 $5.00 Lightweight general purpose Claude Sonnet 4 $3.00 $0.30 $15.00 Mainstream top pick Claude Sonnet 4.5 $3.00 $0.30 $15.00 Mainstream top pick Claude Sonnet 4.6 $3.00 $0.30 $15.00 Mainstream top pick Claude Opus 4.5 $5.00 $0.50 $25.00 Complex arch refactoring Claude Opus 4.6 $5.00 $0.50 $25.00 Complex arch refactoring Claude Opus 4.7 $5.00 $0.50 $25.00 Complex arch refactoring Google Series Gemini 2.5 Pro $1.25 $0.125 $10.00 Powerful reasoning Gemini 3 Flash $0.50 $0.05 $3.00 Fast & lightweight (Preview) Gemini 3.1 Pro $2.00 $0.20 $12.00 Long-context advantage (Preview) xAI Grok Code Fast 1 $0.20 $0.02 $1.50 Ultra-lightweight GitHub Fine-tuned Raptor mini $0.25 $0.025 $2.00 Code optimization (Preview) Goldeneye $1.25 $0.125 $10.00 Code specialized (Preview) Cost Management & Alternatives Hidden Pitfalls and Restrictions Double Billing on Code Reviews: Aside from draining AI Credits, code reviews also eat into your GitHub Actions minutes. Teams working in private repos need to keep an eye on this. Mobile App Subscription Restriction: If you subscribed via the iOS or Android app, you cannot purchase top-up Credits once you run out. Subscribe through the web portal instead. Budget Control Tactics: Set your default model to Grok Code Fast 1 or GPT-5 mini for routine tasks (the lowest cost), and only switch to Sonnet or Opus when it matters. Making good use of cached tokens can cut input costs by 80-90%. Affordable Alternatives: OpenCode Go & Open-Source Ecosystems With mainstream vendors hiking prices, providers from the Chinese open-source ecosystem are gaining traction. OpenCode Go, for instance, charges USD 5 for the first month and gives you access to multiple mainstream models.
Model Name Provider / Series DeepSeek V4 Pro / Flash DeepSeek Qwen 3.5 / 3.6 Plus Alibaba Cloud (Qwen) Kimi K2.5 / K2.6 (3x usage) Moonshot AI (Kimi) GLM-5 / 5.1 DeepInfra, Z.ai MiMo-V2.5 / Pro Xiaomi MiMo MiniMax M2.5 / M2.7 MiniMax For developers on a tight budget, or anyone wanting to try out different model characteristics, platforms like these are a real option next to Copilot.
Enterprise Plan in Practice (June 2026 Update) Enterprise AI Credits are shared across the entire team. In our first week, a 4-person team had already hit the limit. One member used Opus 4.7 a few times, and the AI Credits were gone. I asked two questions this week and got locked out.
Once AI Credits run out, GitHub Copilot's only option is to ask you to purchase more. Given the team size, switching to Claude Code actually gives you more AI Credits to work with. After a few days of use it was noticeably less trouble, and it handled everything we had been giving Copilot.
Conclusion From 2025 to 2026, AI services have moved steadily toward precise per-token billing. As developer demand for tokens rises, higher operating costs follow. A monthly Copilot bill of USD 20 or USD 40 is entirely plausible, especially for anyone leaning on the latest reasoning models.
Token billing has also pushed OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google to put resources into efficient, low-cost small models. However capable a model is, input and output costs that are too high make it unusable, and that pressure drives the industry toward cheaper models.
On the other side, the lower cost floor gives the open-source community and newer vendors an opening. OpenCode Go, Ernie, Qwen, DeepSeek, and Kimi are all climbing, and USD 5 for the first month buys access to several advanced models.
For developers, the most immediate change is that context now has to be budgeted: writing prompts that do more with fewer tokens, using caching to cut redundant tokens, and keeping Agent Mode from quietly expanding costs all become day-to-day concerns.
References Managing your GitHub Copilot billing with AI Credits Models and pricing for GitHub Copilot
title: GitHub Copilot's Shift to AI Credits: 2026 Pricing Analysis and Alternatives

Fair warning: this post stinks. It's a record of a stretch of work with about as low a bar and as little output as I have seen.
Foreword Workplace mishaps come in two kinds. Some are like sudden downpours: you get a bit soaked, you struggle with your umbrella, but it eventually passes. Others are like walking down the street and unexpectedly stepping in a pile of shit. It's not just the dirty shoe; it's that lingering sense of disgust and the self-reproach of "Why didn't I look where I was going?"
When this lands at the end of a long day, right as you're about to pack up, there is genuinely nothing to say. My eyes rolled so far back into my head I could see my brain. So I scribbled this down. Once the frustration settled, the takeaway was simple: now that I know where the shit is, I'll just walk around it next time.
Caught in a shitshow The most draining part is how utterly illogical the mess is.
Sometimes, you expect a path to be smooth, perhaps even scenic. But the moment you plant your foot, that expectation curdles into physical discomfort. That "unintended mess" hits you with the realization that you are burning energy on a completely meaningless drain.
The most frustrating part? Trying to find a way to leap over it or bypass it, only to realize your sole is already stained. All that's left is a sense of hollow defeat.
Stop Trying to "Polish the Turd" Reflecting on it, why was this so particularly revolting?
Because there's no outcome, just a ruined mood. If I'm dealing with something substantial, I'll give it my full respect. But if the content has "negative value," trying to "fix" it is nothing short of a crime against your own life.
Nobody likes stepping in shit. But once the dust settles, I've realized the last thing you should do is pause to analyze the "origin" of the shit, or worse, try to make it smell like roses. What you should do is scrape your boots clean and walk away with grace.
Conclusion So, are you dealing with a "shit mountain" codebase? Or did you, like me, just walk along and step in it?
Now that you know the shit is there, just avoid it next time. As for that mess, leave it right where it is and let it dry out on its own.
title: Don't Polish the Turd: How to Handle the Mess

Introduction I recently got a new keyboard at home. Muscle memory kicked in and I reached for the right Ctrl key—and up popped a Microsoft Copilot window.
Most new Windows laptops and PCs now ship with a Copilot key as standard. If you're someone who habitually uses the right Ctrl with left-hand shortcuts, this change is nothing but a nuisance. Every time your fingers fire on autopilot, the Copilot panel crashes your flow.
Microsoft PowerToys puts it back. The whole setup takes under three minutes.
What Is the Copilot Key? Microsoft officially announced the Copilot key at CES in January 2024, billing it as the most significant keyboard change in nearly 30 years, the biggest since the Windows key was introduced in 1994. Starting in early 2024, major brands like Dell, ASUS, Lenovo, and HP began shipping it on their new Windows 11 laptops, typically in the bottom-right corner, replacing the right Ctrl key.
Under the hood, the Copilot key doesn't send a unique signal. It registers as the keyboard shortcut Win + Shift + F23. Because of this, you need to remap a shortcut, not a key. Simply rebinding F23 alone won't work.
Remapping the Copilot Key with PowerToys The most reliable solution is Microsoft PowerToys 0.98+ and its Keyboard Manager.
PowerToys is a free utility suite built by Microsoft. Beyond remapping shortcuts, it includes plenty of other handy tools.
If you haven't installed PowerToys yet, check out: Awesome Windows—Essential Productivity Software Installation and Guide.
Once it's installed, follow these five steps.
Step 1: Open PowerToys Settings Find the PowerToys icon in the system tray at the bottom-right of your taskbar and double-click it to open Settings.
Step 2: Search for and Open Keyboard Manager In the search bar at the top of the Settings window, type Keyboard, then select Keyboard Manager.
Step 3: Enable Keyboard Manager and Open the New Editor UI On the Keyboard Manager page, make sure the feature is enabled.
Then, it's worth turning on Try the new editor: this is the redesigned Keyboard Manager UI introduced in PowerToys 0.98, and it's easier to work with.
With the new editor enabled, key remaps and shortcut remaps are managed in a single unified interface. Just click the editor button to access both. If you're on the older UI, scroll down to the Shortcuts section and click Remap a shortcut instead.
Step 4: Add a New Remap In the shortcut remapping list, click the ＋ Add remapping button in the top-left corner.
Step 5: Configure the Mapping Rule Set up the new mapping rule as follows:
Field Value Shortcut (trigger) Win (Left) + Shift (Left) + F23 Action (mapped to) Ctrl (Left) When you're done, click Save.
💡 About "Allow chording": Chording is an advanced feature that lets you use a shortcut combination as a prefix, followed by a second key to trigger different actions, great for grouping related functions together. For example, from the official docs: Shift + Ctrl + V → U to increase volume, Shift + Ctrl + V → D to decrease it. In that scenario, Shift + Ctrl + V becomes the shared prefix for all volume controls. For our Ctrl remapping here, it makes no difference whether you enable it or not.
The change takes effect immediately. No reboot required.
Verifying It Works Once configured, open any browser window and use the Copilot key to try Ctrl (Copilot Key) + + and Ctrl (Copilot Key) + -. If the page zooms in and out normally, the remap is working.
Configuration Summary Step Action 1 Open PowerToys Settings 2 Search "Keyboard," open Keyboard Manager 3 Enable the feature, turn on the new editor UI, click Remap a shortcut 4 Add a new shortcut remapping 5 Set trigger to Win + Shift + F23, action to Ctrl (Left), then Save Closing Thoughts Takes less than three minutes to set up, but the interruptions it saves you add up. Microsoft's push to promote AI assistants makes sense from a business standpoint. Copilot on Windows is still genuinely clunky, though, and handing it a key as commonly used as Ctrl leaves me a little speechless. PowerToys is a Microsoft product itself, so fixing this with it is a compromise of sorts.
And this approach isn't just for the Copilot key. If you want to remap any key on your keyboard to a custom function, say turning Caps Lock into Ctrl or mapping a forgotten Scroll Lock key to media controls, PowerToys Keyboard Manager handles that too.
References PowerToys 0.98 is here: new Keyboard Manager UX, the Command Palette Dock and better CursorWrap! Keyboard Manager utility — Microsoft Learn Awesome Windows—Essential Productivity Software Installation and Guide
title: How to Remap the Copilot Key to Ctrl Using PowerToys

Preface The reason for this trip was simple: my company had one spot available for NVIDIA GTC 2026 in San Jose, and I took it. It was my first time visiting the United States. What worried me most before leaving wasn't the itinerary, it was what my family would think, and they turned out to be completely supportive.
GTC essentially took over downtown San Jose: roads were closed, SAP Center was packed with tens of thousands of people, all there for Jensen Huang's two-hour keynote. At the venue, you could turn around at any moment and find yourself next to the CEO of a startup or a leading expert, everyone talking about technologies that are reshaping entire industries. I went feeling excited, but came back with a much clearer sense of what I want to do next.
This post documents what I saw and experienced at GTC, captures impressions from the trip, and reflects on some career-related thoughts.
Itinerary Overview The trip spanned eight days and seven nights, roughly divided into three phases: San Francisco sightseeing, GTC conference, and Silicon Valley exploration.
Date Highlights 3/14 (Sat) Taoyuan → San Francisco: Golden Gate Bridge, Palace of Fine Arts, Union Square 3/15 (Sun) Settle in San Jose, GTC check-in, Welcome Reception 3/16 (Mon) GTC Keynote: Jensen Huang's Opening Address, Humanoid Robot Forum 3/17 (Tue) GTC Exhibition 3/18 (Wed) GTC Forum 3/19 (Thu) GTC Forum, Stanford University, Computer History Museum 3/20 (Fri) Free day, local life experience 3/21 (Sat) San Jose → SFO → Taoyuan Day 1: Taoyuan → San Francisco Departure Early morning at Taoyuan Terminal 2. I boarded an EVA Air Boeing 777 on a direct flight to San Francisco. I browsed the duty-free shops after security, then parked myself at the gate. The 11-hour flight was more manageable than expected. I slept most of it, and when I was awake, I watched Welcome to Derry, which had a good pace. EVA's in-flight meal was up to its usual standard. Somehow it didn't feel that long before we landed.
First Impressions of San Francisco Landing at SFO—my first step on American soil. The feeling was oddly surreal. Customs went smoother than I expected; the questions were basic: how long are you staying, when are you leaving, what brings you here. Simple English got me through. Baggage claim was another story. I waited nearly an hour. Easily the most drawn-out part of the whole arrival.
After the airport, we drove to the hotel to check in and drop off luggage, then headed into the city. First stop: the Golden Gate Bridge.
Golden Gate Bridge Since this was a business trip, there was no time to linger like a proper tourist. I took a few photos, felt the scale in person, then grabbed a latte at a nearby café and moved on (I spent longer ordering the coffee than looking at the bridge).
Seeing it in person is genuinely different from photos. The red steel structure appearing through the Bay Area fog had a presence that no screen can quite replicate.
Palace of Fine Arts Next up: the Palace of Fine Arts. Originally built for the 1915 Panama-Pacific International Exposition, it was later reconstructed and preserved. A beautiful building with great afternoon light, a lake and a lawn around it. It reads more like a park than a monument.
Union Square and the City Next was Union Square in downtown San Francisco. The main goal was the Nintendo Store: walked through, noted that prices are basically higher than Japan, bought nothing.
Walking around, the first thing that made me stop and take a photo wasn't the square itself, but a massive ChatGPT billboard hanging at the most visible spot in the city center. Hard to miss.
Lunch was near Fisherman's Wharf: Clam Chowder in a Bread Bowl, the classic San Francisco dish. Thick clam chowder served inside a hollowed-out sourdough loaf. The bread soaks up the soup, you eat the whole thing together. Salty, comforting, slightly tangy, and the soup-soaked bread is the best part.
After that we wandered around Pier 39. Sea lions were piled up on the wooden docks, completely unbothered by the crowd of tourists watching them.
Checking into San Jose That evening, we drove back to San Jose and returned to Hampton Inn San Jose Cherry Ave, where we'd already checked in that morning. The hotel sits right off Highway 85—heavy traffic in all directions. Getting food meant crossing a massive eight-lane road. The drive to the GTC venue was about 15 minutes, so location was fine overall. Standard American business hotel. Dinner was Panda Express nearby.
My first Panda Express in America. Decent, heavy-flavored, nothing remarkable—it did the job. What caught my eye was the hiring sign on the door, listing salary ranges that reflect the local cost of living:
Position Annual Salary (USD) Approx. TWD General Manager 107K+ ~3.42M Assistant Manager 77K+ ~2.46M Shift Leader & Cook 48K+ ~1.53M Service & Kitchen Team 40K+ ~1.28M Entry-level starting at USD 40K, around TWD 1.28M in Taiwan. That sounds like upper-middle income back home, but in California, after taxes, when a single meal easily runs TWD 400+, this barely qualifies as a living wage. In San Francisco, it might even put you in the low-income bracket.
Day 2: GTC Check-in and Welcome Reception Breakfast and the Neighborhood Hampton Inn includes free breakfast: scrambled eggs, bacon, waffles, juice. There's a self-serve waffle maker: pour the batter in, flip it, done. Simple, filling.
Lunch was a bowl of Vietnamese beef pho at a nearby Pho Kitchen, around TWD 544. Honestly one of the more disappointing meals on the trip. The broth was mediocre, the beef unremarkable. Compared to a random pho shop in Taiwan, this one didn't come close. Very poor value.
On the way out, I noticed a sign in the parking lot warning against smash-and-grab theft, a reminder to keep valuables out of your car.
GTC Check-in In the afternoon, we headed to the San Jose Convention Center to check in. You could spot the GTC event banners hanging from the street lights well before reaching the venue. Inside, I queued at the General Attendees counter, picked up my badge, and got a few drink vouchers with it.
Welcome Reception The GTC welcome reception was, more than anything, a large-scale networking event. The venue served a signature NVIDIA cocktail, the Nvidiarita: green, tasting like a margarita base with something undefined mixed in.
Most people drifted around with drinks, exchanging cards, delivering micro-pitches to potential investors: getting your value proposition across in a few sentences. We naturally ended up talking mostly with people from Asia; the shared background made conversation easier.
Day 3: GTC Keynote, Jensen's Stage The Queue We left early, because Jensen's keynote is the centerpiece of GTC. When we arrived, there was already a long line stretching from the convention center out into the surrounding blocks. Once inside, the sheer scale of an arena that holds tens of thousands of people hit me. Seats were nearly full. The air conditioning was blasting, and after walking around outside all morning, sitting down in there was a relief.
The person seated next to me turned out to be an Asian American who had moved from Beijing at age three, now working on robotics at a startup. One random conversation in a GTC seat, and you're already hearing an interesting story.
Jensen Takes the Stage Being there in person is a completely different experience. The stage presence is undeniable. His pacing, timing of pauses, sense of humor, all calibrated with precision. Yet it never feels rehearsed. There's an engineer's directness underneath everything, a genuine enthusiasm that comes through.
The two-hour keynote didn't have a single dull moment. Jensen went through the growth of the inference market, the hardware spec jumps, the "AI factory" concept that ties compute and storage together, and the Google Cloud partnership at the infrastructure layer.
The takeaway was that NVIDIA is done being only a chip company. Hardware and software ecosystem are being built out together, so that NVIDIA ends up as the infrastructure of the AI era.
Near the end, Jensen started introducing a mascot character—that's when I slipped out early to go take an exam. GTC offers free certification exams during the conference, so I took the NVIDIA NCA-GENL. I wrote a separate post with everything you need to know: NVIDIA NCA-GENL Certification: 20-Minute Passing Guide and Essential Notes.
Humanoid Robot Forum After the keynote, the afternoon session was a humanoid robot expert panel at San Jose Civic, a venue with a great retro theater vibe. Outside, an OpenMind humanoid robot was on display, just sitting there at rest.
Dinner: DoughZone On the way back, I spotted a few cats hanging around by a wooden building—anti-cat spikes were laid out nearby, but the cats had settled in right beside them and didn't care at all.
Dinner was at DoughZone (豆乳坊), a Chinese noodle chain. The soy beef wrap was solid, just slightly awkward eating alone.
Day 4: GTC Exhibition The main event today was the exhibition hall. GTC's exhibition was much larger than I'd imagined, with booths from chip giants to early-stage startups.
Exhibition Highlights ASUS was showcasing AI POD server racks. ASUS is going deeper and deeper into AI infrastructure. Foxconn's booth was impressive too, covering not just servers and infrastructure but also humanoid robot demos.
I stopped by the Microsoft booth and grabbed some Azure-branded snacks. It was much needed. I'd been on my feet all day, and besides the free coffee, the exhibition hall's free Snack Bar (mostly Microsoft-stocked) saved me from hunger more than once.
Session Hopping I spent the day moving between different conference rooms for breakout sessions. The overall feeling was a bit like attending university lectures, sitting in the audience while a presenter walked through their company's technology or research direction.
Some sessions were genuinely valuable, giving you a new perspective to take home. Others didn't land as well—topics too far removed from my current work. One session on the history of CUDA was mostly background and context with little technical substance; I was fighting yawns by the end and left the moment it finished.
Dinner That evening I tried The Kebab Shop and ordered a grilled chicken salad bowl. After several consecutive days of enormous portions, I deliberately went lighter. It was good.
Day 5: AI Forum Face to Face with AI Leaders This was the part of GTC I found most worthwhile.
Visible in the photo: Harrison Chase (LangChain CEO), Mira Murati (former OpenAI CTO), and Aravind Srinivas (Perplexity CEO).
Listening to them discuss their views on the direction of AI, you could feel very directly that these are people who build the thing themselves. The depth of the discussion made me realize how much catching up I still have to do in terms of technical perspective.
Dinner That night I ordered a bacon cheeseburger with cheese fries—the add-on portion was slightly more than I could finish. On the walk back to the hotel I noticed jacaranda trees in full bloom. California's March weather really is something.
Day 6: Stanford University & Computer History Museum Day 6 was the final day of GTC. The exhibition halls and breakout sessions were noticeably smaller in scale, fewer people, and the whole venue had a more open feel. I caught a few morning sessions and called it early.
In the morning, we headed to Stanford University. The campus is enormous. You can just keep walking. We mainly checked out Hoover Tower and the Memorial Court.
Honestly, no overwhelming feeling, just a vast university campus with comfortable weather and good walking. Lunch was Subway, eaten sitting somewhere on campus.
In the afternoon, we drove to Mountain View for the Computer History Museum.
A few exhibits I stood in front of for a long time:
Enigma Cipher Machine (1935)
Enigma was the electromechanical encryption device Germany used heavily through WWII, built from a keyboard, rotors, a plugboard, and a lamp board. The one on display is a 1935 model, close enough to see how the rotors and plugboard were put together.
Bosch ABS Electronic Controller (1978)
Anyone who's worked on automotive electronics will feel something looking at this board. A 1978 ABS control unit PCB—incomparably simpler than today's automotive ECUs, but the foundational concept was laid right here.
The Evolution of Storage
From massive disk platters to IBM RAMAC drives, then optical and floppy disks. Decades of storage evolution compressed onto a single display wall: from kilobytes to terabytes.
Core Memory
A Sperry Rand core memory board and a Whirlwind core plane—up close, those hand-threaded magnetic rings are almost unbelievable. Each tiny ring: one bit. By today's standards it's incomprehensible, but this is where memory started.
A Taiwanese Motherboard
Mid-way through the exhibit, I came across a JoinData 486DX motherboard, labeled Made in Taiwan. Seeing something from home displayed as a historical artifact in a foreign museum was a strange feeling, and it made the "world's contract manufacturer" label feel real. Taiwan's place in the technology chain started right about then.
First-Generation iPhone Teardown
A disassembled display of the original 2007 iPhone components, along with a development board. The moment Jobs unveiled the iPhone changed an entire industry, and these parts are where that change began physically.
Intel Itanium Montecito Wafer
A complete Itanium wafer, packed densely with dies. Itanium ultimately lost to x86-64, but it represents a bold architectural bet.
This museum is the highest-density engineering experience of the entire trip. If you work in software or hardware, or have any interest in the history of computing, set aside half a day for it. If the person you're traveling with isn't an engineer, though, it probably won't land and they'll be bored.
Dinner: La Victoria That night we went to the famous La Victoria Taqueria in San Jose. I ordered the Super Burrito with their iconic orange sauce. The burrito was massive; the orange sauce had a slightly spicy, sweet-tangy kick that worked really well. I still couldn't finish it.
Day 7: Free Day No agenda today. Just wandering through a nearby mall. At some point I walked past a Milksha (迷客夏), a Taiwanese bubble tea chain. Seeing a familiar brand that far from home was a small, genuine surprise. I walked several laps, sat down somewhere when my feet got tired, ordered a drink, and rested.
Later I swung by Trader Joe's to pick up some souvenirs, then ended the night at Jollibee, the Filipino fast food chain that hasn't made it to Taiwan yet. Their signature Chickenjoy fried chicken had crispy skin and juicy meat, a totally different style from KFC, and the portion was more than enough.
Day 8: Heading Home California Sunrise I woke up early on purpose, went out near the hotel, and shot a set of California sunrise photos. The fiery sunrise, the color gradient, the mountain silhouette. The sky cooperated on the last morning.
The weather throughout GTC was all sunshine: around 13°C in the morning, climbing to 30°C by noon, zero clouds. The week after we got back, temperatures started to drop again.
Return Flight We arrived at SFO in the evening and boarded EVA Air back to Taiwan.
Reflections On GTC GTC runs closer to an annual home-turf show than a technical conference. From Jensen's uninterrupted two-hour keynote, to the arms race on the exhibition floor, to what gets discussed in the breakout rooms, you get a very clear sense that AI is already happening rather than coming.
The fact that downtown San Jose closed streets for GTC says everything about the scale and reach. Tens of thousands at the SAP Center keynote, CEOs and experts from around the world, startups lining up to get their demos seen: the energy and scale of this whole ecosystem is genuinely hard to imagine from Taiwan.
On the Gap in Technical Perspective You'll encounter CEOs and technical experts across every field at the venue. These are the people actually steering industries—not short on resources, not lacking direction. Their conversations are about converting the next order-of-magnitude of compute into real solutions, and making AI actually work in concrete real-world scenarios.
What stuck with me most was their attitude toward technical challenges. Whether it's the sustained long-horizon training that AI research demands, or how Agentic AI can autonomously advance and correct itself across multi-step tasks, what they talk about is how to work through it in engineering terms, one step at a time.
What's harder is that hardware is scaling at breakneck speed, but back in actual work environments, market inertia tends to favor conservative, low-cost approaches. Excess compute becomes the reality. The technologies that look electrifying on demo stages often have a much longer road than expected to integrate into existing workflows. That gap is a reality I brought home that still needs facing.
On Career Direction During the trip, a lot of conversations with friends who came along stretched from GTC observations into reflections on where we each are in our work lives. Everyone was at a different position and the views diverged a lot, and much of it only settled for me after I got back.
Some things come down to decisions made above, and you end up starting before the direction is certain. Rather than re-evaluating in place, better to start moving.
Coming back from GTC, I feel more grounded than I did when I left. Direction is clearer. There have always been bottlenecks in my existing technical domain that conventional methods can't break through. But seeing at GTC how AI is being applied in signal processing and decision-layer contexts made me realize this isn't about following a trend or picking an optional add-on. It's the right entry point for solving the hard problems. Worth serious investment.
References NVIDIA GTC 2026 Official Website Computer History Museum NVIDIA NCA-GENL Certification: 20-Minute Passing Guide and Essential Notes
title: NVIDIA GTC 2026: Jensen Huang's Keynote, AI Breakthroughs, and My Silicon Valley Journey
